core_memory.user_feeling_about_friendship: Friendship is a huge topic for me. My closest friends have become my second family at college. They keep me grounded and happy. I was nervous about making friends when I first arrived, but over time, I formed tight bonds that make the stresses of being a CS major manageable.

archival_memory.user_travel_experiences: The user has a travel experience from a sailing trip off the coast of Maine before their sophomore year. They enjoyed exploring New England's coastal towns, sailing past islands, and learning navigation skills from a local instructor. They also mentioned the delicious lobster rolls they had at a dockside shack.
archival_memory.japan_trip: The user visited Tokyo and enjoyed exploring the tech hub, trying Japanese food, and experiencing the bustling streets. They also visited Kyoto, which offered a different vibe of calmness and historical significance. They mentioned visiting shrines and temples, and seeing geishas in Gion. The user felt a sense of stillness and reverence in Kyoto, which left a lasting impression.
archival_memory.family_vacation_europe: The user had a family vacation to Europe where they visited London and Paris. This experience reminded the user of the importance of taking breaks from technology and how it can recharge their energy for programming tasks.

archival_memory.user_talk_about_tony: I should start with my roommate and best friend from freshman year, Tony. We didn't know each other before that first semester, but we clicked right away over this random conversation about a piece of software I was trying to prototype for an Intro to Programming class project. Tony's not even a CS major—he's in mechanical engineering—but we would bounce ideas off each other late into the night, and we realized we had more in common than we initially thought. We both love working with our hands, albeit in different ways: I love to code and design logic, while he loves building things physically. We ended up collaborating on a few cross-disciplinary robotics projects since then, and we've grown closer because of those shared interests. Tony's someone I can always call when I'm overwhelmed with an assignment or if I just want to grab a pizza after a long day.
archival_memory.user_talk_about_sailing_friends: I also have a couple of friends I met through the campus sailing club. You wouldn't believe how many CS students I found there—turns out we like to decompress by hitting the water. It creates this fun mix of personalities: we all share an inclination for problem-solving, so we sometimes treat sailing strategy like a puzzle. The camaraderie on the boat is unlike anything else I've experienced in other clubs. You really have to trust each other out on the water. Our team meets at odd hours(often early in the morning) to catch the best conditions, so we really rely on each other to stay motivated. It's a different kind of bond—there's a deep mutual respect because we see each other's strengths and vulnerabilities in such a high-stakes environment. There's no better feeling than looking across the sailboat and seeing your friend flash you a thumbs-up when you maneuver a particularly tricky tack. One friend, Mariah, has ended up becoming a close confidante for me. She was the one who encouraged me last year to apply for a more challenging research position in data science, telling me I should believe in my skills the way she believed in me. That's the kind of unwavering support we have for each other.
archival_memory.user_talk_about_cs_friends: Of course, as a fourth-year, I've also made plenty of connections through my computer science classes—study groups, group projects, or just the random folks I always saw in the lab at two in the morning, trying to debug code the night before a big assignment. There's this sense of solidarity that comes from those late-night coding sessions—like we're going through the trenches together. I vividly remember this one time in my sophomore year, there was a particularly infamously difficult systems programming course. Our final project was basically building a mini operating system kernel from scratch, and we were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's actually how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We ended up bonding over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?
archival_memory.user_talk_about_gym_friends: Now, I also have some pretty good friends from the gym. Working out has always been an escape for me—I mentioned before that I love to blow off steam by lifting or doing cardio whenever I have a heavy workload. Over time, I kept seeing the same group of people in the early mornings, and it kind of turned into this friendly circle. One of those guys, Dean, is a fellow computer science major, but he's more into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. He and I started talking shop between sets, which led to us comparing notes on our classes, which then led to us being gym buddies who share nutritional tips, workout regimens—pretty much everything. Now, every so often, we'll game together, too. He's the one who got me hooked on a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's become a friendship built around mutual support—pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
archival_memory.user_talk_about_gaming_friends: Speaking of gaming, that's another circle of friends that's quite dear to me. I'm not a hardcore gamer, but I do spend a decent chunk of time on weekends playing multiplayer strategy games, especially when I need a mental break from writing code or reading research papers. We have this informal e-sports club that meets in a common lounge in our student center. I don't always go, but whenever I do, it's guaranteed quality time with friends. There's something special about gaming with a group in the same room—plenty of laughs, random inside jokes, that collective groan when a team fight goes south, and the ultimate hype when we pull off a last-second victory. Actually, I made a great friend, Derek, through that group—he's super skilled in networking security, and he taught me a bunch of techniques that later proved useful in a cybersecurity research project. And the best part is how naturally our friendship evolved—initially from a shared hobby, and later we just kept supporting each other academically.
archival_memory.user_talk_about_library_friend: I should also mention that sometimes friendships can come from the most unexpected places—like the campus library. I spend a fair amount of time there when I want a quieter space to study. You can imagine how loaded my schedule can be as a fourth-year CS major: I'm juggling advanced courses, an intense research project, plus some extracurricular commitments. So the library is often my go-to for a peaceful environment. Over the years, I've bumped into the same faces in the same corner desks. One of those people is Jackson, a law student who somehow ended up reading case studies right next to my stack of cryptography textbooks. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. Over time, we realized we shared an interest in debates—oddly enough, he loves analyzing political and ethical implications of new technologies, so I'd talk to him all day about algorithmic bias. We discovered that, even though we come from different disciplines, we both care about how technology intersects with society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.
archival_memory.user_talk_about_casual_friends: It's not just about the academic or hobby-driven friendships, though. I've made great friends in unexpected, everyday-life situations, like in the dorm laundry room or while waiting in line for coffee. There was this one day when I was super stressed with a research deadline. I was up too late the night before, so I rushed to the campus cafe half-asleep, waiting in a long line. I started complaining—under my breath, but loud enough for the person behind me to hear—about how I needed more time for my research code to run. Turns out, she was also in the thick of her own mechanical engineering lab fiasco. We commiserated, shared a laugh, and ended up sitting together for coffee. That day, we bonded so much over academic stress that we exchanged contact info, and now, whenever we see each other on campus, we make a point to catch up. She might not be a 'best friend' in the sense of constant hangouts, but it's still a positive, supportive relationship that started organically.
archival_memory.user_reflection_on_friendships: I think what unites all these friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're all navigating this crazy journey together. Sometimes, people have this caricature of computer science majors as being antisocial or always stuck behind a screen, but truthfully, my experience has been the opposite. We form these deep connections, especially because the workload and pressure can be so high at times. We're in labs critiquing each other's code, or we're on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to some bug—and those challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.
archival_memory.user_feeling_about_graduation: Now, as a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and that means a lot of goodbyes eventually. I'm excited about the future—internships, job prospects, maybe grad school. But I can't lie: I'm also dreading the day when all these friends I've made scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.
archival_memory.user_reflection_on_friendship_transcendi: In some ways, I think that's what real friendship is: you may not always be geographically close, but you have this strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I learned that from Tony, who's interning across the country this semester, yet we still FaceTime regularly. I see the same dedication in others as well—like Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised that if either of us ends up in Europe, the other has to come visit.
archival_memory.user_feeling_about_friendships: So yeah, I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, random campus encounters—everything. They're truly an integral part of my college experience, and they remind me that there's more to this journey than racking up achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends... that's what success really looks like to me. And I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story—they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
